sections.title: Nvidia faces scrutiny over Megaspeed chip exports
paragraphs: Nvidia is under multiple investigations concerning alleged chip smuggling to China through the Singapore‑based data centre operator Megaspeed[S1][S2][S3]. The U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Nvidia is not the target, but California’s Attorney General, Congress and the SEC are pursuing the matter[S1][S2][S3]. The inquiries focus on what Nvidia knew about the end‑use of its GPUs and whether CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang raised doubts about the company’s assurances[S1].

The U.S. government opened its probe of Megaspeed in 2024, requesting details on Nvidia’s billions of dollars in sales to the firm[S1][S2][S3]. Singapore began its own investigation in 2025, while Megaspeed denies wrongdoing[S1][S2][S3]. Export‑control attorneys note that if Nvidia personnel, from staff to the CEO, had reason to doubt Megaspeed’s statements, the legal risk for Nvidia would increase significantly[S1].

Smuggling and resale of such chips are common challenges for companies like Nvidia, whose products are in high demand for AI workloads[S1][S2][S3]. Compliance relies on assurances from customers, but any indication that those assurances may be unreliable can trigger regulatory scrutiny and potential liability[S1].

sections.title: Character.ai faces legal block on data auction
paragraphs: Character.ai filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2026 and planned to auction its user data, including private chats, to the highest bidder[S4]. A coalition of 42 state attorneys general intervened to stop the sale, arguing it would expose sensitive information without protection[S4][S5].

The AGs say the dataset contains chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, of which over 2.1 million belong to minors, plus IP addresses and other personal data[S4]. The sale would allow the buyer to resell the data without honoring Character.ai's privacy policy, according to the attorneys general[S4][S5]. California Attorney General Rob Bonta called the plan illegal under federal and California law and warned that upcoming chatbot safety legislation in several states could be violated if the auction proceeds[S4][S5].

Bankruptcy courts can order asset sales, but consumer data is typically protected by privacy laws[S4][S5]. Recent state legislation, effective January 1, 2027, aims to regulate chatbot safety and data handling, adding legal risk to the proposed auction[S4]. The AGs' intervention reflects broader scrutiny of AI companies' data practices after multiple investigations into Character.ai's safety record[S5].

sections.title: Amazon and Meta discuss ending Muse shopping block
paragraphs: Amazon and Meta are in talks to allow Meta’s AI shopping assistant Muse to purchase items on Amazon’s marketplace, according to reports from Fortune cited by TechCrunch and The Verge[S6][S7]. The discussions mark a reversal from a block imposed two months earlier that prevented Muse users from checking out on Amazon[S6].

The block was introduced after Muse users received error messages when trying to buy on Amazon, prompting concerns that third‑party agents could divert sales and ad impressions away from Amazon’s own platform[S6]. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has previously argued that few customers complete purchases through external agents, a point that fuels Amazon’s caution about potential revenue loss[S6]. Negotiations focus on product recommendation criteria, the presentation of search results, and the impact on Amazon’s advertising business, which relies on human‑viewed ads across its site[S7]. Both CEOs would need to approve any agreement, and neither company has commented publicly on the talks[S6][S7].

sections.title: Amazon drone crash damages garage in Michigan
paragraphs: The incident began when Jim Brennan and his wife received a notification that their shampoo order would arrive by drone within seven minutes[S9]. After the drone dropped the package, it lost a propeller and became entangled in power lines[S9].

Amazon’s battery‑powered MK30 drones can carry packages up to five pounds and include sense‑and‑avoid technology, yet this drone failed to detect the thin fiber‑optic cable[S9]. The FAA’s preliminary notice described the event as a UAS striking a fiber cable, a residential garage, and power lines during takeoff[S9]. Amazon’s team arrived within ten minutes, coordinated with Detroit Edison, and removed the drone by early evening, offering a $100 gift card and repair assistance[S9].

Prime Air has been expanding aerial deliveries across the United States, but several incidents have drawn regulatory scrutiny[S9]. These events highlight challenges in navigating low‑altitude obstacles despite onboard avoidance systems[S9].
